analysis.one_liner: Bans cargo ships from idling or anchoring off Southern California until the port backlog ends.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with zero cosponsors, never getting a hearing or a vote in the House.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2021 shipping crisis, dozens of cargo ships sat anchored for days or weeks off the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach. This bill would have barred cargo vessels from idling or anchoring in the coastal waters off Southern California until either 180 days after passage or the President declared the port backlog over [S2][S3]. In practice, ships waiting to unload would have had to sail away rather than wait near the coast. The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation Subcommittee, where it stalled and died at the end of the Congress [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of coastal Southern California communities near San Pedro Bay, who live with ship exhaust, noise, and the risk of anchor-drag incidents when dozens of vessels crowd the waters off Long Beach and Los Angeles.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits cargo vessels from idling or anchoring in the coastal waters of Southern California during the backlog period, reducing ship exhaust, noise, and anchoring hazards near coastal communities [S2][S3].
The prohibition lasts until either 180 days after enactment or the day the President determines the backlog at the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach is gone, whichever comes first [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ocean shipping lines, which would lose the ability to wait cheaply near the ports, and the broader supply chain of importers and consumers if ships were forced to leave with cargo still aboard.

drawbacks.text: Banning anchoring does not create port capacity: if ships could not dock, unload, and depart, they would have to idle farther offshore or divert, which could lengthen delivery delays and raise freight costs during a record backlog [S3].
The bill sets no alternative holding areas or enforcement plan for vessels that cannot berth, leaving unresolved how the ban would be carried out at sea [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real, visible problem for coastal communities — ships idling for weeks off Los Angeles and Long Beach — but a blanket ban on waiting offshore did not by itself add dock space, dockworkers, or trucking capacity, so its main practical effect might have been to move the queue somewhere else. It was a narrow, regional response to a supply-chain problem with deeper causes.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its maritime subcommittee without a hearing or a vote, and expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Michelle Steel introduced the bill on October 12, 2021, during the peak of the ship backlog off the Ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach [S1][S5].

It was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure and the next day to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
No other member of the House cosponsored the bill [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Shipping lines and cargo importers benefited, since ships could keep waiting at anchor near the ports without any new restrictions; coastal communities saw no action on ship congestion.

for.name: Rep. Michelle Steel
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban cargo vessels from idling or anchoring off Southern California during the port backlog.

against.name: Peter DeFazio
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee took no action after the bill was referred; it received no hearing or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have taken away their ability to wait cheaply at anchor off Southern California while queueing for berths at Los Angeles and Long Beach. That waiting pushed ship exhaust and anchoring hazards onto nearby coastal communities.

A ban on anchoring could have disrupted delivery of goods during a record backlog, but it also aimed to clear the congestion that was itself delaying cargo. Costs and benefits for shippers were genuinely uncertain.
